{#lep4} # Discussion

{#a0pp} To the best of our knowledge, we firstly produced the weighted pseudo-population by the IPW method, in which the demographic and clinical characteristics were more similar to those of the target RA patients on CREDIT cohort. Moreover, we used the Bootstrap approach to estimate the mean and uncertainty in the annual costs of RA considered their typically right-skewed distribution. The average annual total costs per patient was 41,971 CNY (95%CI: 37,107–47,046 CNY) in our study, in which the direct costs accounted for 75% or over. The medical costs also estimated 28,792 CNY (95%CI: 24,893–33,208 CNY), nearly 89% of direct costs, and even half of them was medication expense. The disease activities, hospitalization, history of comorbidity (e.g., joint replacement or allergy disease), the treatment of biologics or glucocorticoids were found to substantially increase the total costs of RA in China in our study. There also were the significant differences in the geographical distribution of the total cost and the western region were higher than that in the central and eastern regions. All of these results provided a reliable sight into economic burden of RA for the individuals in the real-world clinical practice context of the era of implementing treat-to-targe strategies in China.

{#yt3z} # Introduction

{#qbpc} Rheumatoid arthritis (RA), a progressive inflammatory disease, often leads to joint damage and functional impairment associated with long-term pain and significant disabilities . At global, it affected approximately 0.2–1.0% of the population, with notable regional variations [@w:w1]. In China, the prevalence of rheumatoid arthritis aligns closely with global estimates, whereas its incidence appears modestly higher. [@w:w2]. The most recent large-scale epidemiological study reported an overall prevalence of 368.11 per 100,000 people and an incidence rate of 140.64 per 100,000 person-years in 2017 of China, with a female-to-male ratio of 1.58:1 [@w:w3]. During the past decades, the burden of RA has been on a significant upward trend around the world with 7.4% increase in the global age-standardized prevalence, even faster in mainland of China increased 21.79% per year from 2013 to 2017 [@w:w4]. Given China’s large population, the number of patients with RA might be predicted to keep increasing, account for about one-fourth of the global RA patient population [@w:w5]. Moreover, according to the data of the second nationwide sample survey on disability in China, RA ranked as the second leading cause of disability [@w:w6].

ops.markdown: Nevertheless, several limitations of our study should be acknowledged. First, indirect costs were estimated using the human capital approach, which did not capture the costs of premature retirement due to RA or intangible costs, and therefore might underestimate indirect costs. Second, RA patients frequently carry multiple comorbidities, not all of which are related to RA. Because we captured their total annual healthcare spending, our per-patient costs might overestimate the costs attributable solely to RA. Third, cost estimates relied on patient self-reported data, and there might be recall bias. To maximize accuracy, we invited only patients whose clinical records had been updated by the clinicians they had visited within the previous 30 days, and we asked participants to recall in detail both the expenses of that recent visit and the frequency of visits during the past year. In addition, in the initial stage, 53 patients were randomly selected to report the same information twice within two weeks so that the agreement of the information could be assessed. Fourth, given the cross-sectional design, we could not exclude the possibility of reverse causation or residual confounding; the associations observed between the influence factors and the expenditures of RA therefore warrant confirmation in further prospective cohort studies. Finally, with an overall response rate of only 7%, our cross-sectional study was susceptible to non-response bias. Although IPW mitigated imbalances in observed characteristics, residual confounding from unmeasured factors (such as income and health-seeking behaviors) might persist, potentially limiting the external validity of our findings to the wider RA population.

ops.markdown: To date, evidence on the costs of RA patients in mainland China remains insufficient. The total cost per patient estimated in our study was 41,971 CNY (or $6,507 based on the 2021 RMB to US dollar exchange rate), 0.7 times higher than the $3,826 reported by Xu et al. in 2014 [@w:w34] and 1.7 times higher than the $2,410 (RMB) reported by Hu et al. in 2017 [@w:w35]. These increases mirror the changes in RA management over the past decade. On the one hand, the treatment strategy has shifted toward early T2T, entailing intensive treatment and regular follow-up with the goal of low disease activity or clinical remission [@w:w36], and toward attaining at least 50% improvement in disease activity within 3 months of drug administration [@w:w37]. On the other hand, the introduction of TNF inhibitors, followed by IL-6R inhibitors, abatacept, rituximab and JAK inhibitors, has gradually brought RA treatment in China into the targeted era [@w:w38]. In our study nearly one-quarter of patients received biologic or targeted synthetic therapies, versus only 3% reported by Hu et al [@w:w39]. These advances reduced comorbidity and mortality and helped more patients to achieve drug-maintained remission, but they also increased treatment-related costs. Direct costs dominated the total, of which more than 50% was medication expense, consistent with previous studies in China [@w:w40]. According to the National Bureau of Statistics of China, annual per capita disposable income was 36,883 CNY in 2022 [@w:w41], so the annual direct costs per patient in our study (32,448 CNY) accounted for approximately 88% of that income. Only 17% of our patients reported hospitalization during the last year, making outpatient expenditure the main cost component. Although nearly 67.5% of patients self-reported medical insurance, outpatient expenses were reimbursed in a very low proportion that varied slightly by province [@w:w42]. Cao et al. reported a per-capita cost of $907.78 for RA patients in urban China in 2013–2017 based on a health insurance database; because out-of-pocket payments and patients outside medical insurance were not considered, this figure may underestimate the real-world costs of RA in mainland China [@w:w43]. Overall, most patients had to pay largely out of pocket and therefore face financial hardship from a long-term, incurable disease, particularly those close to or below the poverty line with severe disease and/or comorbidities.
